corrections.source_says: The paper compares two separate class sections and reports no random-assignment procedure. Retain design_class=quasi_people, context_class=observational, and core=no, but describe this as observational context evidence excluded from the core pooled dataset. Under codebook Section 3, non-random comparisons of people belong in observational context; the report-only rule for experiments with fewer than 50 participants specifically concerns randomized experiments.
corrections.quote: This study was conducted with two separate sections of a product development class, taught at Brigham Young University during May and November of 2024.

confirmed: Read the entire 248-line markdown and all 9 PDF pages, including the references; no appendix or supplement is included or mentioned. The title, authors, DOI 10.1017/pds.2025.10342, Proceedings of the Design Society Volume 5: ICED25, and printed pages 3281-3289 support source.version (PDF pp. 1-9).

The paper reports one comparison of two separate BYU class sections taught in May and November 2024; no random-assignment procedure is reported. The quasi_people design and observational context classification are supported, and no randomized people study was found (PDF p. 2, Section 2; full PDF pp. 1-9).

The output analysis covers 39 students: 17 analogue students (3 teams of 4 and 1 team of 5) and 22 ChatGPT students (2 teams of 6 and 2 teams of 5). Table 1 retains those class denominators, supporting n_analyzed=39 and fewer than 50 people; n_randomized appropriately remains null (PDF p. 2, Section 2.1; p. 5, Table 1).
All participants were undergraduates from first to fourth year; approximately 70 percent studied manufacturing, mechanical, or technology engineering (PDF p. 2, Section 2.1).

ChatGPT version 3.5 was used through a shared team laptop, wall-mounted television, and three input keyboards; its class received two additional 1.5-minute demonstration videos. The ideation period was approximately 24 minutes (PDF p. 2, Sections 2 and 2.2.1; p. 3, Section 2.2.2; p. 4, continuation of Section 2.2.2).

Two product-development instructors counted ideas, affinity-mapped idea groups, and original ideas. Ambiguous or incomplete ideas were removed and identical concepts combined; class totals were expressed per student. These are output-based fluency, flexibility, and novelty measures, with set-level reporting (PDF p. 4, Section 2.3.1; p. 5, Section 3.1 and Table 1).
S1-O1 reported values match exactly: ideas per student, Analogue (n = 17) 4.8 and ChatGPT (n = 22) 2.0 (PDF p. 5, Table 1).
S1-O2 reported values match exactly: idea groups per student, Analogue (n = 17) 1.8 and ChatGPT (n = 22) 1.0 (PDF p. 5, Table 1).
S1-O3 reported values match exactly: original ideas per student, Analogue (n = 17) 0.3 and ChatGPT (n = 22) 0.2 (PDF p. 5, Table 1).

The one_line_finding correctly reproduces all six Table 1 values and both class sizes; no SD, SE, confidence interval, or inferential test for these outcomes is reported (PDF p. 5, Table 1; pp. 5-8, Results, Discussion, and Conclusion).

Ancillary samples are smaller: video observations cover 13 analogue and 11 ChatGPT students; the voluntary survey covers 34 of 39 students, with 15 analogue and 19 ChatGPT respondents. These denominators do not replace the Table 1 output-analysis counts (PDF p. 6, Sections 3.2-3.3 and Tables 2-4).

The synthesis defaults are appropriate: Section 2.3 describes evaluation of the current classes, and the discussion compares findings with a prior pilot without reporting a meta-analysis or pooled estimates (PDF p. 4, Section 2.3; p. 7, Section 4.1; p. 8, Conclusion and Bunn et al. 2024 reference).
summary: The full proceedings PDF confirms 39 students, no reported random assignment, and all Table 1 values quoted in the form. Four corrections address incomplete outcome/contrast coding and the report-only eligibility statement, which conflicts with the codebook.
